title: Supplier privilege & architecture deep-dive: assessment template
content:
Purpose:
This template is a working assessment for conducting a technical and contractual review focused on supplier access privileges, system architecture, and the contractual controls needed to enforce least privilege and strong separation of duties. It is intended for security reviewers, SRE/infra, and legal to produce both a technical risk summary and recommended contract language for inclusion in vendor agreements or addenda.

Scope (when to use):
- New supplier onboarding for any partner that will operate runtime inference, manage keys, or have privileged access to customer data.
- Re-assessment for suppliers with architecture changes (new edge components, persistent caches, or support tunnels).
- High-risk pilots where supplier requires broad access for debugging or performance tuning.

How to use this doc:
1) Technical reviewer requests artifacts listed below from supplier.
2) Review items in the checklist and record evidence links (Confluence/GitHub/Jira).
3) Score each section using the scoring rubric.
4) Draft the contract clauses in Section: Recommended contractual language and negotiate with legal/BD.

Required artifacts to request from supplier (minimum):
- High-level architecture diagram showing all network zones, load balancers, NAT, ingress/egress, and data stores.
- Access control matrix (role, privilege, what systems, personnel or service accounts mapped to roles).
- List of service accounts and their ephemeral/permanent nature, plus secret storage locations (KMS/HSM/secret manager).
- Network ACLs, firewall rules and VPC peering configs relevant to the integration.
- Data flow for PII or customer-owned data (where stored, where logged, how masked).
- Incident response and forensic evidence retention document.
- Recent pentest/third-party assessment report (redacted) and remediation ticket list.

Assessment checklist (evidence + questions):
A. Identity & Access (Privilege Matrix)
 - Does supplier provide a role-by-role privilege matrix? (Y/N)
 - Are service accounts distinguished from human operator accounts? (Y/N)
 - Are all privileged actions logged and attributable to an identity? (Evidence: audit log samples)
 - Are there documented processes for temporary elevation, approval workflows and expiry?

B. Secrets & Key Management
 - Where are secrets stored? (KMS/HSM/cloud-secret-manager/local-files)
 - Is key rotation automated? Frequency?
 - Are customer keys ever exported from hardware-backed KMS?
 - Evidence of separation between deploy keys and long-term admin keys.

C. Network & Segmentation
 - Does the supplier isolate customer workloads into separate VPCs/tenants?
 - Are management and debugging interfaces on separate network segments with explicit allow-lists?
 - Does the supplier support IP allow-listing, mutual TLS, or private connectivity (VPC peering, PrivateLink)?

D. Data Flows & Telemetry
 - Which components see unredacted customer data?
 - What telemetry is collected, how long is it retained, and where is it stored?
 - Is PII redacted before logs/telemetry leave customer-controlled boundaries?

E. Operational Controls & Access Reviews
 - Frequency of access reviews and attestation (quarterly, annually).
 - Onboarding/offboarding runbook (time to revoke access).
 - Evidence of privileged session recording or ephemeral bastions.

F. Third-party Dependencies & Build Provenance
 - Are containers and runtime artifacts built in vendor CI or customer-supplied builders?
 - Is there SBOM, code signing, and reproducible build evidence?

G. Forensics & Evidence Preservation
 - Defined retention period for audit logs relevant to incidents.
 - Ability to provide chain-of-custody for logs and backups.

Scoring rubric (quick):
 - 0: No evidence or unacceptable practice.
 - 1: Basic evidence, immature processes, manual controls.
 - 2: Adequate evidence, automated controls for common cases.
 - 3: Strong evidence, automated, tested, and attested controls.

Deliverables from assessment:
 - Technical risk summary (one-paragraph per section with score).
 - Evidence links and redactions performed.
 - Recommended contractual clauses and minimum SLAs.

Recommended contractual language (boilerplate starting points for negotiation):
1) Least Privilege & Access Restrictions (sample clause):
"Supplier shall ensure that access to Customer Data and Customer-controlled infrastructure is provisioned on a least-privilege basis. Supplier will maintain an access control matrix, enforce role-based access controls, and ensure approvals for any temporary elevation. Temporary elevated access will be time-bound, require documented approval from Supplier security, and be automatically revoked after the defined expiry. Supplier shall provide Customer upon request with anonymized attestation logs demonstrating removal of elevated privileges."

2) Architectural Evidence & Review Rights (sample clause):
"Supplier shall provide a current high-level architectural diagram and data flow mapping for Customer review before go-live and upon any material change. Customer reserves the right to request clarification, additional segmentation, or implementation changes to satisfy Customer security requirements. Supplier must notify Customer of architectural changes impacting data residency, access scope, or telemetry collection at least 30 days prior to change; for emergency changes Supplier will notify within 48 hours and follow up with permanent documentation within 5 business days."

3) Separation of Duties & Operator Controls (sample clause):
"Supplier will implement separation of duties for build, deployment, and production operations such that no single individual or service account may both promote code to production and approve access changes. Supplier will maintain logged records of approvals and provide periodic (quarterly) access attestation to Customer."

4) Key Handling & Escrow (sample clause):
"Supplier shall use hardware-backed key management where available and shall not export customer master keys in plaintext. Where supplier requires temporary access to a customer-provided key for support, supplier will use a short-lived wrapping key and document the justification, approval, and automatic expiry. Any key escrow arrangement shall be explicitly scoped, time-bound, and require dual authorization for retrieval."

5) Evidence & Remediation SLA (sample clause):
"Supplier shall retain forensics-grade logs for a minimum period of 90 days (or longer if required by law) and provide prioritized root cause analysis and remediation plan for high severity incidents within 72 hours. Supplier will maintain a remediation SLA for critical security findings with defined timelines and weekly status updates until closure."

Negotiation notes (practical):
- Push for explicit definitions (what counts as privileged access, who is an operator).
- Require minimum automated controls rather than manual attestations for production access.
- If supplier resists architecture review rights, require enhanced telemetry and constrained scope for pilot phases.
- For smaller suppliers, accept phased commitments with milestones tied to go-live (e.g., initial allow-listing + backloged remediation with pen-test evidence required within 90 days).

Appendix: Example evidence checklist to attach to contract negotiation packet:
 - Architecture diagram (annotated)
 - Role & privileges CSV export
 - Sample audit log showing privilege escalation and expiry
 - Secret rotation policy and cryptographic key lifecycle table
 - Pentest report + remediation ticket list
 - Incident response runbook excerpt

Reviewer quick template (paste into assessment):
- Supplier name: 
- Product/Service: 
- Assessor: 
- Assessment date: 
- Summary score (0-3 per section): Identity/Secrets/Network/Data/Operations/Third-party/Forensics
- High risk items (top 3): 
- Recommended contractual additions (top 3): 

This document is intended as a working template. Tailor the sample clauses to the specific legal jurisdiction and business model; legal counsel should review before committing to live contracts.
